html:
The Mogollon culture was a farming culture of the mountains and deserts of what is now southwestern New Mexico, southeastern Arizona and northern Mexico, from about 200 to 1450. The map shows it in 800 and 900.

Mogollon people farmed maize, beans and squash and also hunted and gathered. For centuries they lived in pit houses, partly sunk into the ground. Later they built above ground pueblos of stone and adobe, much like their neighbours the Ancestral Puebloans to the north. The Hohokam lived to their west.

Their best known art is the pottery of the Mimbres valley, made between about 1000 and 1130: white bowls painted in black with people, animals and geometric designs. Many were buried with the dead, upside down over the face, with a hole punched in the bottom.

Later Mogollon people may have been part of the rise of Paquimé in Chihuahua. The name comes from the Mogollon Mountains, named after a Spanish governor of New Mexico in the 1700s.
